questions.prompt: Complete: "My sister and I delivered the bread, and the baker paid ___ before closing."
questions.explanation: "us" is the object pronoun of we, and an object pronoun stands after the verb: the baker paid us. "we" is the subject form and belongs before the verb, "our" is a possessive adjective and needs a noun straight after it, and "them" would point at other people instead of the two who did the work.

questions.prompt: Which of these words can stand immediately before a noun, as in "___ uniform"?
questions.explanation: "her" is right: a possessive adjective is the only form that can stand immediately before a noun, and her is the possessive of the she-row — her uniform. "she" is a subject pronoun and stands before a verb, "him" is an object pronoun and stands after a verb or a preposition, and "they" is a subject pronoun as well.

questions.prompt: Your classmate wants to say what his mother does for a living. Which sentence is correct English?

options.text: Is a nurse in a big hospital.
She a nurse in a big hospital.
She's a nurse in a big hospital.
Her is a nurse in a big hospital.

questions.explanation: "She's a nurse in a big hospital." is right: English never drops the subject, and She's is simply the short form of She is. "Is a nurse in a big hospital." leaves the sentence with no subject at all, "She a nurse in a big hospital." drops the verb, and "Her is a nurse in a big hospital." uses her, which is the object and possessive form, where the subject belongs.

questions.prompt: Which pair of prepositions completes this sentence? "The new cookery course begins ___ September, and the first class is ___ Tuesday."
questions.explanation: "in / on" is right: a month takes in, which gives in September, and a day of the week takes on, which gives on Tuesday. "at / on" opens with at, the preposition of a clock time such as at seven; "in / at" puts at in front of a day; and "on / in" swaps the two, which would give on September and in Tuesday.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The number of guests ___ the weather, so nobody can promise a figure."
questions.explanation: "depends on" is right: the verb depend always travels with the same preposition, on — the number of guests depends on the weather. "depends of" copies a preposition from another language, "depends from" borrows the preposition of origin, and "depends about" borrows the preposition of a subject you talk about.
